article.headline: A Feedback Loop for Teaching Yourself to Prompt Better
article.lede: Most people who use Claude regularly assume their prompts are working. The article by @itsolelehmann argues otherwise: roughly 30% of Claude interactions quietly fail, producing plausible-looking but flawed output that users accept without scrutiny. The proposed fix is a structured self-improvement loop borrowed from the research habits of AI scientist Andrej Karpathy.
article.body:
The core mechanism is what the author calls *autoresearch* — an automated feedback cycle in which an AI agent is given a task, its output is evaluated against a ground-truth or rubric, failures are logged, and the agent then researches its own gaps and rewrites the relevant instructions or prompts. Run in a loop, the idea is that a skill's weak points surface and are patched without the user having to notice or diagnose them manually. The image attached to the quoted tweet shows the expected learning curve: slow improvement with conventional effort, then a steeper climb once the loop is running.

Andrej Karpathy — a co-founder of OpenAI, former head of AI at Tesla, and one of the most widely followed practitioners in the field — has publicly explored workflows in which language models iteratively critique and improve their own outputs. The article applies that sensibility to everyday prompting: rather than grinding through trial and error, you instrument the failure mode and let the system close the loop for you.

**"Intelligence tokens"** is the author's term for the context-window capacity consumed each time you invoke a model — a proxy for cost and attention. The claim is that most of those tokens are wasted on prompts that are structurally flawed in repeatable ways. Better prompts mean the same token budget produces more reliable results, hence "ROI on your intelligence tokens."

The article is pitched at Claude users specifically, but the underlying logic applies to any large language model workflow. The key constraint it sidesteps is human blind-spot: people tend not to notice when an AI gives a confident wrong answer, especially in domains where they lack deep expertise. An automated evaluator, by contrast, can catch systematic errors that a busy practitioner would miss entirely.

The research sources returned for this bookmark did not include the full article text, so the 30% failure-rate figure and the precise mechanics of the loop cannot be independently verified here. That number is a claim in the article, not a published benchmark.

concepts.definition: A workflow in which an AI agent completes a task, has its output evaluated against a standard, identifies where it fell short, researches those gaps, and updates its own instructions — then repeats. The goal is self-directed skill improvement without manual intervention.

An informal term for the context-window tokens consumed when prompting a large language model. Because LLMs charge by token or have fixed context limits, getting useful output per token is a form of efficiency. 'ROI on intelligence tokens' means extracting more reliable results from the same budget.

When a language model produces an answer that looks correct but contains errors the user doesn't catch — often because the prompt was ambiguous, the model hallucinated confidently, or the user lacked domain expertise to spot the problem. These failures are called 'silent' because they don't produce an obvious error message.

article.fact_check: The 30% failure-rate figure cited in the article headline is an assertion, not a published or peer-reviewed measurement. Without the full article text being available in the research sources, it cannot be verified. Readers should treat it as a motivating estimate rather than an empirical benchmark. The attribution to 'Karpathy's autoresearch method' is also informal; Karpathy has publicly discussed iterative AI workflows, but there is no single published paper or named method of his that carries this label.
